title: India and Japan Just Signed Their First Defence Co-Development Deal. It Is the Start of Something Much Bigger.
excerpt: Modi and Takaichi summit in New Delhi delivered pacts on AI, stealth naval tech, critical minerals, and a $61 billion investment roadmap — reshaping what the two economies mean to each other.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India and Japan signed their first defence co-development agreement during Takaichi's visit.
  • The UNICORN project will enhance India's naval capabilities with Japanese technology.
  • Bilateral trade reached $27.5 billion in fiscal year 2025-26, with $3.2 billion in Japanese investments.
  • Both nations aim to attract $61 billion in Japanese investment over the next decade.
  • The partnership opens new career opportunities for Indian professionals in tech and defence.
Strengthening Defence Ties
›First-ever defence co-development agreement signed.
›UNICORN project focuses on naval radar technology.
›India is second to receive Japanese defence tech.
›Partnership aims to enhance regional peace and security.
When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi arrived in New Delhi on July 1 for a three-day state visit, the atmospherics suggested something beyond routine diplomacy. She was accorded a full ceremonial welcome at Rashtrapati Bhavan — and by the time she departed, India and Japan had signed their first-ever defence co-development agreement, a stack of AI and energy pacts, and a joint roadmap for economic security that reads like a blueprint for a new kind of Asian partnership. The centrepiece is the UNICORN project — the co-development of a Unified Complex Radio Antenna for Indian Navy warships. Originally designed by Japan's NEC Corporation and deployed on its Mogami-class frigates, the stealth-capable radar mast integrates multiple antennas into a single structure, reducing a ship's radar cross-section. India's Bharat Electronics Limited will handle integration and co-production. "This project will open a new chapter in our defence technology partnership," Modi told reporters. "We will now jointly develop defence technologies that strengthen regional peace, maritime security, and the rules-based order." It is worth pausing on what this means. Japan's post-war pacifist constitution long barred meaningful arms exports. India is only the second country — after the Philippines — to receive Japanese defence technology under Tokyo's recently relaxed export rules. The signal to Beijing is unmistakable: two of Asia's largest democracies are now co-developing military hardware. ## Beyond Defence: AI, Minerals, and the Investment Pipeline The 16th Annual Summit produced agreements across a sweep of strategic sectors. A joint statement on artificial intelligence commits both countries to combining Japan's precision technology with India's software capabilities — a pairing Modi called a potential "new momentum for global AI development." Separate pacts cover semiconductors, quantum technologies, critical minerals, and next-generation mobility. Japan pledged to set up 1,000 biogas and organic fertiliser plants in India under a new bio-gas initiative, aimed at rural livelihoods and India's clean-energy transition. A declaration on economic security formalised cooperation on supply-chain resilience — an area where both countries want to reduce dependence on China for everything from rare earths to pharmaceutical ingredients. Bilateral trade reached $27.5 billion in fiscal year 2025-26. Japanese investment in India totalled $3.2 billion between April and December 2025 alone, and over the past year roughly 120 new business agreements have been concluded, bringing an estimated $10 billion in fresh Japanese investment. But the headline target is larger still: India and Japan aim to attract 10 trillion yen — roughly $61 billion — in Japanese investment and double the number of Japanese companies operating in India over the next decade. About 1,400 Japanese firms are already active in the country, nearly half in manufacturing. ## Healthcare and the Bullet Train The summit expanded cooperation in pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and biotechnology. "By combining India's scale with Japan's quality, we will work towards delivering affordable, reliable and advanced health solutions to the world," Modi said. Japan remains the key backer of India's most ambitious infrastructure project — the Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train corridor, the country's first high-speed rail link. Japanese firms have also made high-profile bets on Indian financial institutions, including a recent $1.6 billion deal for a 20% stake in Yes Bank.

Takaichi framed the partnership in explicitly strategic terms. "Amid a turbulent international landscape, building such a mutually complementary cooperative relationship has become increasingly important," she said. The summit also reaffirmed both countries' commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific through the Quad grouping with the United States and Australia. ## What This Means for the Diaspora For Indian professionals in tech and defence, the India-Japan corridor is becoming a serious career and investment pathway. The UNICORN project alone will require cross-border engineering talent. The AI cooperation framework opens doors for Indian software engineers collaborating with Japanese precision-tech firms. The 10 trillion yen investment target means new manufacturing and technology jobs across India — and with Japan's ageing workforce, Indian talent is increasingly in demand in Tokyo, Osaka, and beyond. For NRI investors, the expanding bilateral relationship creates opportunities in sectors from defence manufacturing to clean energy. Modi is now heading to Indonesia, Australia, and New Zealand next week, continuing an aggressive diplomatic calendar. But the Japan summit stands out: it represents a fundamental upgrade in what two of Asia's largest economies can build together — from warships to biogas plants, from semiconductor supply chains to hospital equipment.
Expanding Opportunities for Indian Professionals
›UNICORN project requires cross-border engineering talent.
›AI cooperation opens doors for Indian software engineers.
›Investment target creates new manufacturing jobs.
›Japanese firms seek Indian talent due to an ageing workforce.
The economics of Japan-India relations have never been deeper. The question now is whether the bureaucracies and businesses on both sides can move as fast as the political will suggests. *Sources: Reuters, The Business Standard, GKToday, News89, Observer Research Foundation, India Strategic*
